Spatial Weights and Applications

Author

Davin Cuaso

Published

14 September 2026

Modified

19 September 2026

Overview

I follow Chapter 8: Spatial Weights and Applications and the Lesson 4 outline. Using GDP per capita (GDPPC, measured in RMB) for 88 counties in Hunan, China, I answer four questions:

  1. How does the definition of a neighbour change the spatial weights matrix?
  2. How does row standardisation turn those links into comparable weights?
  3. Which counties stand out after their GDPPC is compared with neighbouring counties?
  4. How do local summary statistics vary across the province?

Data and preparation

I use the files distributed with the current course’s Lesson 4 rather than recreating the data from another source.

Dataset Source Use
Hunan county boundary Official Lesson 4 course files Polygons and neighbourhood relationships
Hunan 2012 development indicators Official Lesson 4 course file County GDP per capita
Hunan variable dictionary Professor-provided Lesson 4 dictionary Defines GDPPC as gross domestic product per capita in RMB

The dictionary identifies GDPPC as gross domestic product per capita in RMB and rates its data completeness as good. The shapefile and CSV both carry a County field. I use that field as the join key instead of relying on row order. A left join keeps all 88 polygons and attaches the indicators. The final table retains the three administrative identifiers, the common county name and four development measures required later in the exercise.

Show the R code 
hunan_boundary <- st_read(
  dsn = file.path(data_path, "geospatial"),
  layer = "Hunan",
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_make_valid()

hunan_2012 <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_path, "aspatial", "Hunan_2012.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

hunan <- hunan_boundary |>
  left_join(hunan_2012, by = "County") |>
  select(NAME_2, ID_3, NAME_3, County, GDPPC, GIO, Agri, Service)

stopifnot(
  nrow(hunan_boundary) == 88,
  nrow(hunan_2012) == 88,
  nrow(hunan) == 88,
  n_distinct(hunan$County) == 88,
  !anyNA(hunan$GDPPC)
)

input_summary <- data.frame(
  Check = c(
    "County polygons",
    "Indicator rows",
    "Matched GDPPC values",
    "Retained analysis fields",
    "Geometry type",
    "Coordinate reference system"
  ),
  Result = c(
    nrow(hunan_boundary),
    nrow(hunan_2012),
    sum(!is.na(hunan$GDPPC)),
    paste(setdiff(names(hunan), attr(hunan, "sf_column")), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(hunan))), collapse = ", "),
    st_crs(hunan)$input
  )
)

kable(input_summary, caption = "Input validation before constructing spatial weights")

Check Result
County polygons 88
Indicator rows 88
Matched GDPPC values 88
Retained analysis fields NAME_2, ID_3, NAME_3, County, GDPPC, GIO, Agri, Service
Geometry type POLYGON

GDP per capita

Show the R code 
tm_shape(hunan) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "GDPPC",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      n = 5,
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.purples"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "GDPPC (RMB)",
      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")
    ),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.4
  ) +
  tm_title("GDP per capita by county, Hunan Province") +
  tm_credits(
    "Source: ISSS626 Lesson 4 course files and variable dictionary",
    position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom")
  )

The quantile classes follow the choropleth workflow used in Exercise 1b. They divide the counties into similarly sized groups, which makes the geographic ranking easy to read. The legend sits outside the map frame, so it does not cover any counties. The distribution is right-skewed: the median GDPPC is 20,433, while the maximum is 88,656.

Contiguity-based neighbours

poly2nb() derives neighbours directly from the polygon topology. Under the queen rule, counties are neighbours when their boundaries share either an edge or a corner. The stricter rook rule requires a shared edge.

Show the R code 
queen_nb <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = TRUE, row.names = hunan$County)
rook_nb <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = FALSE, row.names = hunan$County)

neighbour_summary <- function(nb, method) {
  counts <- card(nb)
  data.frame(
    Method = method,
    `Directed links` = sum(counts),
    `Average neighbours` = round(mean(counts), 2),
    `Minimum neighbours` = min(counts),
    `Maximum neighbours` = max(counts),
    `Connected components` = n.comp.nb(nb)$nc,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

contiguity_summary <- bind_rows(
  neighbour_summary(queen_nb, "Queen contiguity"),
  neighbour_summary(rook_nb, "Rook contiguity")
)

kable(contiguity_summary, caption = "Contiguity neighbour structures")
Contiguity neighbour structures
Method Directed links Average neighbours Minimum neighbours Maximum neighbours Connected components
Queen contiguity 448 5.09 1 11 1
Rook contiguity 440 5.00 1 10 1

Queen contiguity produces 448 directed links and an average of 5.09 neighbours per county. Rook contiguity produces 440 links. The small difference means that most connections come from shared edges; only a few exist solely because two counties meet at a corner.

Show the R code 
centres <- suppressWarnings(st_centroid(hunan))
coords <- st_coordinates(centres)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.4, 0.4, 2.2, 0.4))
plot(st_geometry(hunan), col = "#f3f4f6", border = "white", main = "Queen contiguity")
plot(queen_nb, coords, add = TRUE, col = "#2563eb", lwd = 0.6, pch = 19, cex = 0.35)
plot(st_geometry(hunan), col = "#f3f4f6", border = "white", main = "Rook contiguity")
plot(rook_nb, coords, add = TRUE, col = "#dc2626", lwd = 0.6, pch = 19, cex = 0.35)
Show the R code 
par(old_par)

Reading one neighbour list

The first polygon is Anxiang. Its list entry stores the row numbers of all counties connected under the queen rule.

Show the R code 
anxiang_id <- match("Anxiang", hunan$County)
anxiang_neighbour_ids <- queen_nb[[anxiang_id]]

anxiang_neighbours <- data.frame(
  County = hunan$County[anxiang_neighbour_ids],
  GDPPC = hunan$GDPPC[anxiang_neighbour_ids]
) |>
  arrange(County)

kable(
  anxiang_neighbours,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  caption = "Anxiang's queen-contiguity neighbours"
)
Anxiang’s queen-contiguity neighbours
County GDPPC
Hanshou 20,981
Jinshi 34,592
Li 24,473
Nan 21,311
Taoyuan 22,879

Distance-based neighbours

Contiguity may not represent every kind of interaction. The chapter therefore introduces two distance-based alternatives. I retain its 62 km fixed band, which gives every county at least one neighbour and keeps the province in a single connected component. I also construct a six-nearest-neighbour graph, which gives every county the same number of outgoing links.

Show the R code 
distance_62_nb <- dnearneigh(
  coords,
  d1 = 0,
  d2 = 62,
  row.names = hunan$County,
  longlat = TRUE
)

knn6_nb <- knn2nb(
  knearneigh(coords, k = 6, longlat = TRUE),
  row.names = hunan$County
)

distance_summary <- bind_rows(
  neighbour_summary(distance_62_nb, "Fixed distance: 62 km"),
  neighbour_summary(knn6_nb, "Six nearest neighbours")
)

kable(distance_summary, caption = "Distance-based neighbour structures")
Distance-based neighbour structures
Method Directed links Average neighbours Minimum neighbours Maximum neighbours Connected components
Fixed distance: 62 km 324 3.68 1 6 1
Six nearest neighbours 528 6.00 6 6 1

The 62 km band yields 324 directed links, fewer than either contiguity rule. The six-nearest-neighbour graph yields 528 directed links because every county selects six neighbours. Its links are not necessarily symmetric: county A can rank B among its six closest counties even when B does not rank A among its own six.

Show the R code 
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.4, 0.4, 2.2, 0.4))
plot(st_geometry(hunan), col = "#f3f4f6", border = "white", main = "Within 62 km")
plot(distance_62_nb, coords, add = TRUE, col = "#0f766e", lwd = 0.6, pch = 19, cex = 0.35)
plot(st_geometry(hunan), col = "#f3f4f6", border = "white", main = "Six nearest neighbours")
plot(knn6_nb, coords, add = TRUE, col = "#7c3aed", lwd = 0.6, pch = 19, cex = 0.35)
Show the R code 
par(old_par)

From neighbours to weights

A neighbour list only records who is connected. nb2listw() assigns numeric weights to those links. Binary weights give every neighbour a value of 1. Row-standardised weights divide each row by its number of neighbours, so the weights for each county add to 1. Inverse-distance weights give closer neighbours more influence before the same row standardisation is applied.

Show the R code 
queen_binary <- nb2listw(queen_nb, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
queen_row <- nb2listw(queen_nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

queen_distances <- nbdists(queen_nb, coords, longlat = TRUE)
inverse_distance <- lapply(queen_distances, function(x) 1 / x)
queen_idw <- nb2listw(
  queen_nb,
  glist = inverse_distance,
  style = "W",
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

anxiang_weights <- data.frame(
  County = hunan$County[anxiang_neighbour_ids],
  `Distance (km)` = round(queen_distances[[anxiang_id]], 1),
  Binary = queen_binary$weights[[anxiang_id]],
  `Row-standardised` = round(queen_row$weights[[anxiang_id]], 3),
  `Row-standardised inverse distance` = round(queen_idw$weights[[anxiang_id]], 3),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  arrange(County)

kable(anxiang_weights, caption = "How Anxiang's queen neighbours are weighted")
How Anxiang’s queen neighbours are weighted
County Distance (km) Binary Row-standardised Row-standardised inverse distance
Hanshou 65.1 1 0.2 0.137
Jinshi 25.5 1 0.2 0.349
Li 54.9 1 0.2 0.162
Nan 35.6 1 0.2 0.250
Taoyuan 87.4 1 0.2 0.102

For Anxiang, ordinary row standardisation gives each of its 5 neighbours a weight of 0.2. The inverse-distance version still sums to 1, but gives a larger share to nearer county centres. Row standardisation is useful for a neighbouring average; binary weights are appropriate when the desired quantity is a neighbouring sum.

Spatially lagged GDPPC

The spatial lag is the weighted combination of neighbouring values. With row-standardised queen weights, it is the mean GDPPC among a county’s neighbours.

Show the R code 
hunan$lag_gdppc <- lag.listw(
  queen_row,
  hunan$GDPPC,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

hunan$neighbour_sum <- lag.listw(
  queen_binary,
  hunan$GDPPC,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

queen_self_nb <- include.self(queen_nb)
queen_self_row <- nb2listw(queen_self_nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
queen_self_binary <- nb2listw(queen_self_nb, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)

hunan$window_average <- lag.listw(
  queen_self_row,
  hunan$GDPPC,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

hunan$window_sum <- lag.listw(
  queen_self_binary,
  hunan$GDPPC,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

hunan$own_minus_lag <- hunan$GDPPC - hunan$lag_gdppc

lag_examples <- hunan |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(
    County,
    GDPPC,
    lag_gdppc,
    neighbour_sum,
    window_average,
    window_sum
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(GDPPC - lag_gdppc))) |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), round))

kable(
  lag_examples,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  caption = "Counties with the largest absolute gap from their neighbours"
)
Counties with the largest absolute gap from their neighbours
County GDPPC lag_gdppc neighbour_sum window_average window_sum
Lengshuijiang 64,257 14,419 43,258 26,879 107,515
Changsha 88,656 41,364 248,182 48,120 336,838
Zixing 65,706 20,269 141,883 25,949 207,589
Pingjiang 17,252 55,158 220,631 47,577 237,883
Ningxiang 62,202 33,583 235,079 37,160 297,281
Wangcheng 70,666 45,651 273,907 49,225 344,573
Guidong 8,497 32,671 98,013 26,628 106,510
Zhuzhou 27,589 47,346 284,074 44,523 311,663

These four lags answer different questions:

  • lag_gdppc is the average among neighbours only.
  • neighbour_sum adds neighbouring GDPPC values, so it increases with both values and neighbour count.
  • window_average averages the county together with its neighbours.
  • window_sum adds the county to the neighbouring sum.

The window average is less extreme than the neighbour-only comparison because it includes the county’s own value. The sums should not be interpreted as local income totals; they are included to demonstrate how the choice of binary versus row-standardised weights changes the calculation.

Show the R code 
map_comparison <- bind_rows(
  hunan |>
    select(County, value = GDPPC) |>
    mutate(Measure = "County GDPPC"),
  hunan |>
    select(County, value = lag_gdppc) |>
    mutate(Measure = "Average neighbour GDPPC")
) |>
  mutate(Measure = factor(
    Measure,
    levels = c("County GDPPC", "Average neighbour GDPPC")
  ))

ggplot(map_comparison) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = value), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~Measure) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "C",
    limits = range(hunan$GDPPC),
    breaks = c(20000, 50000, 80000),
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    name = "GDPPC"
  ) +
  guides(fill = guide_colourbar(
    title.position = "top",
    barwidth = grid::unit(10, "cm"),
    barheight = grid::unit(0.35, "cm")
  )) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

The neighbour map is smoother because each value is an average of several counties. The correlation between own and neighbouring GDPPC is 0.485: nearby counties tend to be similar, but the relationship is far from perfect.

Counties that differ from their neighbours

Show the R code 
label_counties <- hunan |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  slice_max(abs(own_minus_lag), n = 8)

ggplot(st_drop_geometry(hunan), aes(x = lag_gdppc, y = GDPPC)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey55", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = own_minus_lag), size = 2.4, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text(
    data = label_counties,
    aes(label = County),
    colour = "grey20",
    size = 3.1,
    nudge_y = 1800,
    check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_colour_gradient2(
    low = "#2563eb",
    mid = "grey80",
    high = "#dc2626",
    midpoint = 0,
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    name = "Own minus\nneighbour GDPPC"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = "Average neighbour GDPPC",
    y = "County GDPPC",
    title = "Some counties are very different from their surroundings",
    subtitle = "The dashed line marks equality between own and neighbouring GDPPC"
  )

Lengshuijiang, Changsha and Zixing sit well above their surrounding averages. Pingjiang is the strongest contrast in the other direction: its GDPPC is much lower than the average among its queen-contiguous neighbours. These local comparisons identify places worth examining in a later spatial-autocorrelation analysis. They are not significance tests.

Geographically weighted summary statistics

GWmodel still expects an older Spatial object for these functions, so I convert the joined sf object only at this point. The main data object remains in sf format for importing, joining, mapping and spatial weights.

The adaptive bandwidth is selected by leave-one-out cross-validation with bw.gwr(). I use the local regression GDPPC ~ GIO + Agri + Service because those four measures were retained during data preparation. The returned bandwidth is a neighbour count, not a distance in kilometres. I then use the same adaptive bisquare kernel for the local summary statistics.

Show the R code 
hunan_sp <- as(hunan, "Spatial")

adaptive_bw <- bw.gwr(
  GDPPC ~ GIO + Agri + Service,
  data = hunan_sp,
  approach = "CV",
  kernel = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = TRUE
)
Adaptive bandwidth: 62 CV score: 9486953536 
Adaptive bandwidth: 46 CV score: 9612120071 
Adaptive bandwidth: 72 CV score: 9453498415 
Adaptive bandwidth: 78 CV score: 9429123115 
Adaptive bandwidth: 82 CV score: 9417452507 
Adaptive bandwidth: 84 CV score: 9433230785 
Adaptive bandwidth: 80 CV score: 9418552223 
Adaptive bandwidth: 82 CV score: 9417452507
Show the R code 
gw_summary <- gwss(
  hunan_sp,
  vars = c("GDPPC", "GIO", "Agri", "Service"),
  bw = adaptive_bw,
  kernel = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  quantile = TRUE,
  longlat = TRUE
)

gwss_df <- as.data.frame(gw_summary$SDF) |>
  select(GDPPC_LM, GDPPC_Median, Corr_GDPPC.Agri)

stopifnot(
  nrow(gwss_df) == nrow(hunan),
  identical(rownames(gwss_df), rownames(hunan_sp@data))
)

hunan_gwss <- bind_cols(hunan, gwss_df)

bandwidth_check <- data.frame(
  Item = c("Bandwidth method", "Kernel", "Adaptive nearest neighbours"),
  Value = c("Leave-one-out cross-validation", "Bisquare", adaptive_bw)
)

kable(bandwidth_check, caption = "Bandwidth used for geographically weighted summaries")
Bandwidth used for geographically weighted summaries
Item Value
Bandwidth method Leave-one-out cross-validation
Kernel Bisquare
Adaptive nearest neighbours 82

Cross-validation selects 82 nearest neighbours. This is a fairly broad local window for a dataset of 88 counties, so the estimates should be read as regional patterns rather than highly local detail. Strictly speaking, bw.gwr() optimises the predictive fit of the stated GWR equation. It does not directly optimise the local mean or median. Reusing the bandwidth keeps the kernel definition consistent, but it is still a modelling choice.

Show the R code 
observed_map <- tm_shape(hunan_gwss) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "GDPPC",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      n = 5,
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.oranges"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Observed GDPPC",
      position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom")
    ),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.3
  ) +
  tm_title("Observed GDPPC")

local_mean_map <- tm_shape(hunan_gwss) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "GDPPC_LM",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      n = 5,
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.blues"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Local mean GDPPC",
      position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom")
    ),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.3
  ) +
  tm_title("Geographically weighted mean")

local_median_map <- tm_shape(hunan_gwss) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "GDPPC_Median",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      n = 5,
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.greens"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Local median GDPPC",
      position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom")
    ),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.3
  ) +
  tm_title("Geographically weighted median")

tmap_arrange(observed_map, local_mean_map, local_median_map, ncol = 3)

The local mean and median maps are smoother than the observed map because every estimate combines nearby counties. The median is less affected by unusually high GDPPC values. It is therefore a useful check on whether a local mean is being pulled upward by one prosperous county.

Show the R code 
tm_shape(hunan_gwss) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "Corr_GDPPC.Agri",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      n = 7,
      style = "pretty",
      midpoint = 0,
      values = "brewer.rd_bu"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Local correlation",
      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")
    ),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.3
  ) +
  tm_title("GDPPC and agriculture do not relate uniformly across Hunan")

The local correlation is descriptive. It shows where GDPPC and agricultural output move together within the adaptive kernel, but it does not show that one variable causes the other. Results can also change when the bandwidth, kernel or variables in the bandwidth-selection model change.

Assumptions and limits

  • A queen link assumes that any shared edge or corner can support interaction. A different substantive process may call for rook, road-network or travel-time neighbours.
  • The distance methods use polygon centroids. Large or irregular counties are reduced to one representative point, and the 62 km threshold is a connectivity rule rather than an economic boundary.
  • Six-nearest-neighbour links impose equal outgoing neighbour counts even where settlement density differs. They can also be asymmetric.
  • Row standardisation gives every county the same total weight, which increases the individual influence of neighbours around counties with few links.
  • GDPPC is a county-level, cross-sectional indicator. A spatial lag describes context; it does not show that neighbouring GDPPC caused a county’s value.
  • The adaptive bandwidth is selected for the GWR equation and then reused for the summary statistics. A bandwidth chosen for a different equation could produce a different local pattern.
  • GWmodel requires the temporary conversion from sf to Spatial. Row order is preserved during the conversion and checked before the GWSS results are attached.

What I found

Changing the neighbour rule changes the graph, even though the 88 county values stay the same. I use queen contiguity as the main specification because the question concerns counties that touch. With row-standardised weights, each spatial lag is the mean among those neighbours. Lengshuijiang, Changsha and Zixing are well above their surrounding averages, while Pingjiang is well below. The geographically weighted mean and median add a broader regional view, using an adaptive bandwidth selected by cross-validation. All of these results are descriptive. They do not show that one county’s GDPPC caused another’s.

## Overview

I follow [Chapter 8: Spatial Weights and Applications](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap08.html) and the [Lesson 4 outline](https://isss626-ay2026-27aug.netlify.app/outline/lesson04_outline). Using GDP per capita (GDPPC, measured in RMB) for 88 counties in Hunan, China, I answer four questions:

1. How does the definition of a neighbour change the spatial weights matrix?
2. How does row standardisation turn those links into comparable weights?
3. Which counties stand out after their GDPPC is compared with neighbouring counties?
4. How do local summary statistics vary across the province?

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

pacman::p_load(
  sf, ggstatsplot, tmap, tidyverse, knitr, GWmodel, spdep
)

options(scipen = 999)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
tmap_mode("plot")
data_path <- "data"
```

## Data and preparation

I use the files distributed with the current course's Lesson 4 rather than recreating the data from another source.

| Dataset | Source | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Hunan county boundary | [Official Lesson 4 course files](https://github.com/tskam/ISSS626-AY2026-27Aug/tree/master/lesson/Lesson04/data/geospatial) | Polygons and neighbourhood relationships |
| Hunan 2012 development indicators | [Official Lesson 4 course file](https://github.com/tskam/ISSS626-AY2026-27Aug/blob/master/lesson/Lesson04/data/aspatial/Hunan_2012.csv) | County GDP per capita |
| Hunan variable dictionary | [Professor-provided Lesson 4 dictionary](data/aspatial/Dictionary.xlsx) | Defines GDPPC as gross domestic product per capita in RMB |

The dictionary identifies GDPPC as gross domestic product per capita in RMB and rates its data completeness as good. The shapefile and CSV both carry a `County` field. I use that field as the join key instead of relying on row order. A left join keeps all 88 polygons and attaches the indicators. The final table retains the three administrative identifiers, the common county name and four development measures required later in the exercise.

```{r}
#| label: import-and-join

hunan_boundary <- st_read(
  dsn = file.path(data_path, "geospatial"),
  layer = "Hunan",
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_make_valid()

hunan_2012 <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_path, "aspatial", "Hunan_2012.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

hunan <- hunan_boundary |>
  left_join(hunan_2012, by = "County") |>
  select(NAME_2, ID_3, NAME_3, County, GDPPC, GIO, Agri, Service)

stopifnot(
  nrow(hunan_boundary) == 88,
  nrow(hunan_2012) == 88,
  nrow(hunan) == 88,
  n_distinct(hunan$County) == 88,
  !anyNA(hunan$GDPPC)
)

input_summary <- data.frame(
  Check = c(
    "County polygons",
    "Indicator rows",
    "Matched GDPPC values",
    "Retained analysis fields",
    "Geometry type",
    "Coordinate reference system"
  ),
  Result = c(
    nrow(hunan_boundary),
    nrow(hunan_2012),
    sum(!is.na(hunan$GDPPC)),
    paste(setdiff(names(hunan), attr(hunan, "sf_column")), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(hunan))), collapse = ", "),
    st_crs(hunan)$input
  )
)

kable(input_summary, caption = "Input validation before constructing spatial weights")
```

### GDP per capita

```{r}
#| label: gdppc-map
#| fig-cap: "GDP per capita by Hunan county, 2012"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

tm_shape(hunan) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "GDPPC",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      n = 5,
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.purples"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "GDPPC (RMB)",
      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")
    ),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.4
  ) +
  tm_title("GDP per capita by county, Hunan Province") +
  tm_credits(
    "Source: ISSS626 Lesson 4 course files and variable dictionary",
    position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom")
  )
```

The quantile classes follow the choropleth workflow used in Exercise 1b. They divide the counties into similarly sized groups, which makes the geographic ranking easy to read. The legend sits outside the map frame, so it does not cover any counties. The distribution is right-skewed: the median GDPPC is `r scales::comma(median(hunan$GDPPC))`, while the maximum is `r scales::comma(max(hunan$GDPPC))`.

## Contiguity-based neighbours

`poly2nb()` derives neighbours directly from the polygon topology. Under the **queen** rule, counties are neighbours when their boundaries share either an edge or a corner. The stricter **rook** rule requires a shared edge.

```{r}
#| label: contiguity-weights

queen_nb <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = TRUE, row.names = hunan$County)
rook_nb <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = FALSE, row.names = hunan$County)

neighbour_summary <- function(nb, method) {
  counts <- card(nb)
  data.frame(
    Method = method,
    `Directed links` = sum(counts),
    `Average neighbours` = round(mean(counts), 2),
    `Minimum neighbours` = min(counts),
    `Maximum neighbours` = max(counts),
    `Connected components` = n.comp.nb(nb)$nc,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

contiguity_summary <- bind_rows(
  neighbour_summary(queen_nb, "Queen contiguity"),
  neighbour_summary(rook_nb, "Rook contiguity")
)

kable(contiguity_summary, caption = "Contiguity neighbour structures")
```

Queen contiguity produces `r sum(card(queen_nb))` directed links and an average of `r round(mean(card(queen_nb)), 2)` neighbours per county. Rook contiguity produces `r sum(card(rook_nb))` links. The small difference means that most connections come from shared edges; only a few exist solely because two counties meet at a corner.

```{r}
#| label: contiguity-network
#| fig-cap: "Queen contiguity (left) retains corner contacts that rook contiguity (right) excludes"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

centres <- suppressWarnings(st_centroid(hunan))
coords <- st_coordinates(centres)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.4, 0.4, 2.2, 0.4))
plot(st_geometry(hunan), col = "#f3f4f6", border = "white", main = "Queen contiguity")
plot(queen_nb, coords, add = TRUE, col = "#2563eb", lwd = 0.6, pch = 19, cex = 0.35)
plot(st_geometry(hunan), col = "#f3f4f6", border = "white", main = "Rook contiguity")
plot(rook_nb, coords, add = TRUE, col = "#dc2626", lwd = 0.6, pch = 19, cex = 0.35)
par(old_par)
```

### Reading one neighbour list

The first polygon is Anxiang. Its list entry stores the row numbers of all counties connected under the queen rule.

```{r}
#| label: anxiang-neighbours

anxiang_id <- match("Anxiang", hunan$County)
anxiang_neighbour_ids <- queen_nb[[anxiang_id]]

anxiang_neighbours <- data.frame(
  County = hunan$County[anxiang_neighbour_ids],
  GDPPC = hunan$GDPPC[anxiang_neighbour_ids]
) |>
  arrange(County)

kable(
  anxiang_neighbours,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  caption = "Anxiang's queen-contiguity neighbours"
)
```

## Distance-based neighbours

Contiguity may not represent every kind of interaction. The chapter therefore introduces two distance-based alternatives. I retain its **62 km fixed band**, which gives every county at least one neighbour and keeps the province in a single connected component. I also construct a **six-nearest-neighbour** graph, which gives every county the same number of outgoing links.

```{r}
#| label: distance-weights

distance_62_nb <- dnearneigh(
  coords,
  d1 = 0,
  d2 = 62,
  row.names = hunan$County,
  longlat = TRUE
)

knn6_nb <- knn2nb(
  knearneigh(coords, k = 6, longlat = TRUE),
  row.names = hunan$County
)

distance_summary <- bind_rows(
  neighbour_summary(distance_62_nb, "Fixed distance: 62 km"),
  neighbour_summary(knn6_nb, "Six nearest neighbours")
)

kable(distance_summary, caption = "Distance-based neighbour structures")
```

The 62 km band yields `r sum(card(distance_62_nb))` directed links, fewer than either contiguity rule. The six-nearest-neighbour graph yields `r sum(card(knn6_nb))` directed links because every county selects six neighbours. Its links are not necessarily symmetric: county A can rank B among its six closest counties even when B does not rank A among its own six.

```{r}
#| label: distance-network
#| fig-cap: "A fixed distance band (left) versus six nearest neighbours (right)"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.4, 0.4, 2.2, 0.4))
plot(st_geometry(hunan), col = "#f3f4f6", border = "white", main = "Within 62 km")
plot(distance_62_nb, coords, add = TRUE, col = "#0f766e", lwd = 0.6, pch = 19, cex = 0.35)
plot(st_geometry(hunan), col = "#f3f4f6", border = "white", main = "Six nearest neighbours")
plot(knn6_nb, coords, add = TRUE, col = "#7c3aed", lwd = 0.6, pch = 19, cex = 0.35)
par(old_par)
```

## From neighbours to weights

A neighbour list only records who is connected. `nb2listw()` assigns numeric weights to those links. Binary weights give every neighbour a value of 1. Row-standardised weights divide each row by its number of neighbours, so the weights for each county add to 1. Inverse-distance weights give closer neighbours more influence before the same row standardisation is applied.

```{r}
#| label: weight-styles

queen_binary <- nb2listw(queen_nb, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
queen_row <- nb2listw(queen_nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

queen_distances <- nbdists(queen_nb, coords, longlat = TRUE)
inverse_distance <- lapply(queen_distances, function(x) 1 / x)
queen_idw <- nb2listw(
  queen_nb,
  glist = inverse_distance,
  style = "W",
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

anxiang_weights <- data.frame(
  County = hunan$County[anxiang_neighbour_ids],
  `Distance (km)` = round(queen_distances[[anxiang_id]], 1),
  Binary = queen_binary$weights[[anxiang_id]],
  `Row-standardised` = round(queen_row$weights[[anxiang_id]], 3),
  `Row-standardised inverse distance` = round(queen_idw$weights[[anxiang_id]], 3),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  arrange(County)

kable(anxiang_weights, caption = "How Anxiang's queen neighbours are weighted")
```

For Anxiang, ordinary row standardisation gives each of its `r card(queen_nb)[anxiang_id]` neighbours a weight of `r round(1 / card(queen_nb)[anxiang_id], 2)`. The inverse-distance version still sums to 1, but gives a larger share to nearer county centres. Row standardisation is useful for a neighbouring **average**; binary weights are appropriate when the desired quantity is a neighbouring **sum**.

## Spatially lagged GDPPC

The spatial lag is the weighted combination of neighbouring values. With row-standardised queen weights, it is the mean GDPPC among a county's neighbours.

```{r}
#| label: spatial-lags

hunan$lag_gdppc <- lag.listw(
  queen_row,
  hunan$GDPPC,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

hunan$neighbour_sum <- lag.listw(
  queen_binary,
  hunan$GDPPC,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

queen_self_nb <- include.self(queen_nb)
queen_self_row <- nb2listw(queen_self_nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
queen_self_binary <- nb2listw(queen_self_nb, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)

hunan$window_average <- lag.listw(
  queen_self_row,
  hunan$GDPPC,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

hunan$window_sum <- lag.listw(
  queen_self_binary,
  hunan$GDPPC,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

hunan$own_minus_lag <- hunan$GDPPC - hunan$lag_gdppc

lag_examples <- hunan |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(
    County,
    GDPPC,
    lag_gdppc,
    neighbour_sum,
    window_average,
    window_sum
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(GDPPC - lag_gdppc))) |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), round))

kable(
  lag_examples,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  caption = "Counties with the largest absolute gap from their neighbours"
)
```

These four lags answer different questions:

- `lag_gdppc` is the average among neighbours only.
- `neighbour_sum` adds neighbouring GDPPC values, so it increases with both values and neighbour count.
- `window_average` averages the county together with its neighbours.
- `window_sum` adds the county to the neighbouring sum.

The window average is less extreme than the neighbour-only comparison because it includes the county's own value. The sums should not be interpreted as local income totals; they are included to demonstrate how the choice of binary versus row-standardised weights changes the calculation.

```{r}
#| label: own-and-lag-map
#| fig-cap: "Observed GDPPC and the row-standardised queen spatial lag use the same colour scale"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5

map_comparison <- bind_rows(
  hunan |>
    select(County, value = GDPPC) |>
    mutate(Measure = "County GDPPC"),
  hunan |>
    select(County, value = lag_gdppc) |>
    mutate(Measure = "Average neighbour GDPPC")
) |>
  mutate(Measure = factor(
    Measure,
    levels = c("County GDPPC", "Average neighbour GDPPC")
  ))

ggplot(map_comparison) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = value), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~Measure) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "C",
    limits = range(hunan$GDPPC),
    breaks = c(20000, 50000, 80000),
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    name = "GDPPC"
  ) +
  guides(fill = guide_colourbar(
    title.position = "top",
    barwidth = grid::unit(10, "cm"),
    barheight = grid::unit(0.35, "cm")
  )) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

The neighbour map is smoother because each value is an average of several counties. The correlation between own and neighbouring GDPPC is `r round(cor(hunan$GDPPC, hunan$lag_gdppc), 3)`: nearby counties tend to be similar, but the relationship is far from perfect.

### Counties that differ from their neighbours

```{r}
#| label: lag-comparison
#| fig-cap: "GDPPC compared with the average of queen-contiguous neighbours"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

label_counties <- hunan |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  slice_max(abs(own_minus_lag), n = 8)

ggplot(st_drop_geometry(hunan), aes(x = lag_gdppc, y = GDPPC)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey55", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = own_minus_lag), size = 2.4, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text(
    data = label_counties,
    aes(label = County),
    colour = "grey20",
    size = 3.1,
    nudge_y = 1800,
    check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_colour_gradient2(
    low = "#2563eb",
    mid = "grey80",
    high = "#dc2626",
    midpoint = 0,
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    name = "Own minus\nneighbour GDPPC"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = "Average neighbour GDPPC",
    y = "County GDPPC",
    title = "Some counties are very different from their surroundings",
    subtitle = "The dashed line marks equality between own and neighbouring GDPPC"
  )
```

Lengshuijiang, Changsha and Zixing sit well above their surrounding averages. Pingjiang is the strongest contrast in the other direction: its GDPPC is much lower than the average among its queen-contiguous neighbours. These local comparisons identify places worth examining in a later spatial-autocorrelation analysis. They are not significance tests.

## Geographically weighted summary statistics

`GWmodel` still expects an older `Spatial` object for these functions, so I convert the joined `sf` object only at this point. The main data object remains in `sf` format for importing, joining, mapping and spatial weights.

The adaptive bandwidth is selected by leave-one-out cross-validation with `bw.gwr()`. I use the local regression `GDPPC ~ GIO + Agri + Service` because those four measures were retained during data preparation. The returned bandwidth is a neighbour count, not a distance in kilometres. I then use the same adaptive bisquare kernel for the local summary statistics.

```{r}
#| label: gwss-bandwidth

hunan_sp <- as(hunan, "Spatial")

adaptive_bw <- bw.gwr(
  GDPPC ~ GIO + Agri + Service,
  data = hunan_sp,
  approach = "CV",
  kernel = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = TRUE
)

gw_summary <- gwss(
  hunan_sp,
  vars = c("GDPPC", "GIO", "Agri", "Service"),
  bw = adaptive_bw,
  kernel = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  quantile = TRUE,
  longlat = TRUE
)

gwss_df <- as.data.frame(gw_summary$SDF) |>
  select(GDPPC_LM, GDPPC_Median, Corr_GDPPC.Agri)

stopifnot(
  nrow(gwss_df) == nrow(hunan),
  identical(rownames(gwss_df), rownames(hunan_sp@data))
)

hunan_gwss <- bind_cols(hunan, gwss_df)

bandwidth_check <- data.frame(
  Item = c("Bandwidth method", "Kernel", "Adaptive nearest neighbours"),
  Value = c("Leave-one-out cross-validation", "Bisquare", adaptive_bw)
)

kable(bandwidth_check, caption = "Bandwidth used for geographically weighted summaries")
```

Cross-validation selects `r adaptive_bw` nearest neighbours. This is a fairly broad local window for a dataset of 88 counties, so the estimates should be read as regional patterns rather than highly local detail. Strictly speaking, `bw.gwr()` optimises the predictive fit of the stated GWR equation. It does not directly optimise the local mean or median. Reusing the bandwidth keeps the kernel definition consistent, but it is still a modelling choice.

```{r}
#| label: gwss-maps
#| fig-cap: "Observed GDPPC and geographically weighted GDPPC summaries"
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6

observed_map <- tm_shape(hunan_gwss) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "GDPPC",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      n = 5,
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.oranges"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Observed GDPPC",
      position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom")
    ),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.3
  ) +
  tm_title("Observed GDPPC")

local_mean_map <- tm_shape(hunan_gwss) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "GDPPC_LM",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      n = 5,
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.blues"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Local mean GDPPC",
      position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom")
    ),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.3
  ) +
  tm_title("Geographically weighted mean")

local_median_map <- tm_shape(hunan_gwss) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "GDPPC_Median",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      n = 5,
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.greens"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Local median GDPPC",
      position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom")
    ),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.3
  ) +
  tm_title("Geographically weighted median")

tmap_arrange(observed_map, local_mean_map, local_median_map, ncol = 3)
```

The local mean and median maps are smoother than the observed map because every estimate combines nearby counties. The median is less affected by unusually high GDPPC values. It is therefore a useful check on whether a local mean is being pulled upward by one prosperous county.

```{r}
#| label: gw-correlation-map
#| fig-cap: "Local Pearson correlation between GDPPC and gross agricultural output"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

tm_shape(hunan_gwss) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "Corr_GDPPC.Agri",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      n = 7,
      style = "pretty",
      midpoint = 0,
      values = "brewer.rd_bu"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Local correlation",
      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")
    ),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.3
  ) +
  tm_title("GDPPC and agriculture do not relate uniformly across Hunan")
```

The local correlation is descriptive. It shows where GDPPC and agricultural output move together within the adaptive kernel, but it does not show that one variable causes the other. Results can also change when the bandwidth, kernel or variables in the bandwidth-selection model change.

## Assumptions and limits

- A queen link assumes that any shared edge or corner can support interaction. A different substantive process may call for rook, road-network or travel-time neighbours.
- The distance methods use polygon centroids. Large or irregular counties are reduced to one representative point, and the 62 km threshold is a connectivity rule rather than an economic boundary.
- Six-nearest-neighbour links impose equal outgoing neighbour counts even where settlement density differs. They can also be asymmetric.
- Row standardisation gives every county the same total weight, which increases the individual influence of neighbours around counties with few links.
- GDPPC is a county-level, cross-sectional indicator. A spatial lag describes context; it does not show that neighbouring GDPPC caused a county's value.
- The adaptive bandwidth is selected for the GWR equation and then reused for the summary statistics. A bandwidth chosen for a different equation could produce a different local pattern.
- `GWmodel` requires the temporary conversion from `sf` to `Spatial`. Row order is preserved during the conversion and checked before the GWSS results are attached.

## What I found

Changing the neighbour rule changes the graph, even though the 88 county values stay the same. I use queen contiguity as the main specification because the question concerns counties that touch. With row-standardised weights, each spatial lag is the mean among those neighbours. Lengshuijiang, Changsha and Zixing are well above their surrounding averages, while Pingjiang is well below. The geographically weighted mean and median add a broader regional view, using an adaptive bandwidth selected by cross-validation. All of these results are descriptive. They do not show that one county's GDPPC caused another's.
